tasks.title: Expose the confirmed RuntimeIdentity contract
tasks.objective: Give every public client the user-confirmed Provider-neutral RuntimeIdentity shape, including explicit identity persistence, build target facts, and version-number capabilities.
tasks.outcome: Rust, TypeScript, and CLI clients observe one exact RuntimeIdentity contract and can distinguish identity lifetime, compatibility, platform, architecture, and supported capability versions without probing private implementation details.
acceptance: The public contract exposes exactly `daemonInstanceId: string`, `runtimeId: string`, `runtimeIdPersistence: "daemon" | "state_dir"`, `buildId: string`, `protocolGeneration: number`, `platform: string`, `arch: string`, and `capabilities: Record<string, number>`; Rust protocol truth, generated TypeScript declarations, runtime validation, client projections, CLI JSON, and documentation agree on those fields.

`runtimeId` remains distinct from daemon incarnation, Run, Provider, build, host, and credential identity. `runtimeIdPersistence` is `daemon` for a memory-only Runtime ID that lasts one daemon lifetime and `state_dir` for a Runtime ID preserved by the selected state-directory lineage across cold replacement; validated planned exec preserves the Runtime and daemon identities.

`buildId`, `platform`, and `arch` are daemon-authored serving-build facts. `platform` is exactly `std::env::consts::OS` and `arch` is exactly `std::env::consts::ARCH` (for example `macos` and `aarch64` on an Apple Silicon macOS build), not Node/release names. These facts are not Git or binary attestation, host fingerprinting, credentials, Provider identity, endpoint discovery, or transport negotiation.

The initial flat capability catalog is exactly `native.start`, `native.recoverable_input`, `native.fork_level_a`, `native.execute_materialized_level_b`, `tmux.discover`, `tmux.import`, `services.persistent_state`, and `services.planned_exec_upgrade_continuity`. A Runtime advertises only fully implemented keys; version `1` names the currently implemented public contract for each advertised initial key, and absence means unsupported.

Each capability value and client requirement is a JavaScript-safe positive integer in `1..=9_007_199_254_740_991` naming the highest fully implemented version for that exact key. Zero, negative, fractional, boolean, string, null, array, nested-object, overflow, and platform/executable-inferred values fail closed in Rust and TypeScript. A request for an absent key or a version above the advertised value returns an explicit `unsupported_capability` result without fallback.

Capability requirements are client-local compatibility preconditions: the Rust client builder and TypeScript client options accept exact required key/version pairs, compare them after Hello and before sending any business Request or Attach frame, and do not add requirements to the wire. Rust `ping` and `runtime_info`, TypeScript `runtimeInfo`, and CLI auto-start readiness remain raw identity inspection paths so an incompatible live Runtime can be diagnosed without replacement.

Rust and TypeScript mock peers prove absent and higher-version requirements close before a business frame; real memory-only public-client fixtures prove no Run is created on rejection. Real memory-only, persistent cold-replacement, and planned-exec fixtures prove the identity and persistence discriminator lifecycle, and the CLI remains a client of the Rust public boundary.

No plugin discovery, marketplace, embedded runtime, capability negotiation, transport negotiation framework, Provider catalog, operation-to-key inference, key normalization, or host credential surface is introduced. Any change to the confirmed fields, discriminators, initial flat keys, safe-integer version semantics, Rust target vocabulary, or client-local pre-dispatch requirement boundary requires explicit user confirmation and a later reviewed Feature Tracker plan revision before implementation.

verification.proves: Exact RuntimeIdentity schema, cross-language and CLI parity, safe-integer capability negatives, client-local absent/higher rejection before dispatch, identity lifecycles, public clients, and repository regressions pass.
RuntimeIdentity fields, lifecycle, build-target facts, numeric capability versions, unsupported behavior, and non-goals have one public protocol owner.
The direct user-confirmed initial key catalog, numeric domain, Rust target vocabulary, client-local requirement boundary, and change-control rule are durably bound to plan revision 3.

Snapshot, attach, event, list, status, fork, cold recovery, and exec-upgrade paths agree on revision and timestamp truth.

tasks.title: Provide race-safe TypeScript Runtime activation
tasks.objective: Expose a framework-neutral TypeScript helper that connects to or activates one compatible local ctxmux Runtime while the daemon remains the Run owner.
tasks.outcome: An embedding product can activate, prove readiness, exit, and later reconnect without private spawning logic or coupling daemon life to Node.
acceptance: Concurrent activators converge on one compatible Runtime or return a typed conflict using public identity and readiness, not fixed sleeps.
Live, stale, ordinary-file, symlink, permission, timeout, crashed-launcher, and incompatible-Runtime cases never kill or replace an unrelated target.

The helper exposes explicit executable, socket, state, environment, deadline, and child-disposition inputs and performs no download, global mutation, credential handling, Electron coupling, or SSH fallback.
The activating Node process may exit while daemon-owned Runs survive and a fresh clean consumer reconnects to the same Run and replay.

verification.proves: Activation races, socket safety, readiness, compatibility, caller-exit survival, and SDK regressions pass.
Activation inputs, lifecycle, errors, security boundary, and non-goals are consumer-visible.
